hero.headline: Federal judge blocks Trump immigration policies affecting 39 countries
hero.body:
A federal judge ruled on Friday that the Trump administration unlawfully barred applicants from 39 travel-ban countries from receiving decisions on asylum, work permits, green cards and citizenship applications.

The judge found that the administration lacked legal authority to implement the broad suspension of immigration processing. The ruling requires Trump officials to restart the decision-making process for applications that had been frozen, affecting people from countries including Cuba, Haiti, and Venezuela.

The decision marks a significant setback for the administration's immigration agenda. The judge's order takes effect immediately, meaning immigration officials must begin processing applications and making decisions for nationals of all 39 targeted countries. The suspension had prevented thousands of pending cases from moving forward and blocked new applicants from these nations from filing altogether.

The Trump administration had imposed the immigration freeze as part of a broader effort to restrict entry from dozens of nations. Immigration advocates challenged the policy shortly after its implementation, arguing it violated existing immigration law and due process protections.

Legal experts noted the ruling could affect thousands of cases that have been on hold. Many states base their vaccine recommendations and insurance coverage directly on federal guidance, so changes in policy can have widespread effects across the country.

The administration has pursued numerous policies to limit immigration and asylum access, many of which have faced legal challenges. This ruling follows a pattern of federal courts blocking or narrowing immigration restrictions that judges found exceeded executive authority or violated statutory requirements.

An HHS spokesperson responded to the decision, saying "HHS looks forward to this judge's decision being overturned just like his other attempts to keep the Trump administration from governing."

The judge's ruling came on the same day the US Senate voted to pass legislation funding Donald Trump's controversial immigration enforcement expansion. The Senate approved the $70 billion bill in a 52-47 vote early Friday morning, ending a partial government shutdown that had lasted since February. The measure provides funding for US Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the Department of Homeland Security for three years. No Democrats voted for the legislation.

Though Trump officials may appeal the court's decision blocking the immigration freeze, the immediate effect requires them to resume accepting and processing applications from nationals of all 39 countries. The outcome will likely depend on how higher courts handle any appeals, though legal experts remain uncertain how appellate judges will rule on the case.

cards.headline: Iran strikes US military base in Kuwait, killing one and injuring dozens
cards.body:
Iran launched a military strike on a US military facility at Kuwait International Airport, resulting in one death and dozens of injuries. The attack represents an escalation in the ongoing US-Iran conflict and threatens to undermine ceasefire efforts in the Middle East.

The strike targeted American military personnel stationed at the airport, which serves both civilian and military functions. The incident occurred as tensions between Washington and Tehran continue to simmer following months of military exchanges. In recent weeks, both countries have launched strikes against each other, though neither side has achieved a decisive advantage.

This latest Iranian attack comes amid nuclear negotiations between the US and Iran. Donald Trump's administration has indicated it is considering limited military strikes as leverage in talks. Trump gave Iran a deadline of 10 to 15 days to reach a nuclear agreement or face what he called "really bad things." When asked about potential strikes, Trump told reporters: "I guess I can say I am considering" it.

Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said there is no military solution to the nuclear dispute. He noted that despite previous attacks on Iranian facilities and the assassination of scientists, such actions had failed to stop Iran's nuclear programme. Araghchi indicated his government would have a counterproposal ready within days following indirect talks held in Geneva this week with Trump's envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner.

The US military presence in Kuwait operates under longstanding defense arrangements between Washington and the Gulf nation. The strike on this key American ally highlights the precarious regional situation. A ceasefire between the US and Iran, which came into effect in April, has held only partially. Earlier flare-ups over recent months were quickly contained, but analysts warn the ceasefire risks becoming another Middle East stalemate with significant economic and political consequences.

Multiple obstacles complicate peace prospects. Iran doubts Trump's ability to deliver or maintain any agreement, fearing the US will simply walk away again as it did from the previous nuclear deal during Trump's first presidency. The US insists Iran cannot possess nuclear weapons or the capacity to build them and cannot enrich uranium.

Meanwhile, Israel and Lebanon agreed to renew their ceasefire this week, adding another layer to the complex regional dynamics. However, Lebanese leaders have criticized Iran, stating their country should not be used as a bargaining chip in broader disputes between larger powers.

The attack on US forces in Kuwait complicates ongoing diplomatic efforts and raises questions about how Washington will respond to direct strikes on its military personnel in allied territory. The incident demonstrates how fragile the current ceasefire arrangement remains and the difficulty both sides face in moving from military confrontation toward genuine peace negotiations.

cards.headline: Trump envoys meet with nuclear experts on potential Iran negotiations
cards.teaser: Presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner traveled to Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee on Thursday to consult with technical experts who cou.
cards.body:
Presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee on Thursday to meet with technical experts who could assist in future nuclear negotiations with Iran. The White House is preparing groundwork for potential diplomatic talks as it seeks to address concerns about Iran's nuclear program.

The laboratory's specialized expertise in nuclear technology and weapons development makes it a strategic resource for any diplomatic effort. The high-level visit signals that the Trump administration is taking concrete preparatory steps toward engagement, with technical experts expected to play a crucial role in verifying compliance and analyzing Iran's capabilities during negotiations.

cards.headline: Putin declines meeting with Zelensky to discuss ending Ukraine war
cards.teaser: The Russian president rejected a call for face-to-face talks after his Ukrainian counterpart wrote an open letter proposing direct negotiations.
cards.body:
Vladimir Putin has rejected Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky's open letter calling for face-to-face negotiations. Speaking at the St. Petersburg economic forum, Putin described the letter as rude and said he sees "no point" in meeting with Zelensky to discuss ending the conflict.

Putin reaffirmed Russia's war objectives, stating the country will achieve its goals in Ukraine, including seizing the eastern Donbas region. At the same forum, Russian business and political elites debated whether Russia should halt the conflict or continue military operations, though Putin's remarks suggested he intends to press forward with the war.

cards.headline: US Employers Added 172,000 Jobs in May as Labor Market Extends Rebound
cards.body:
American employers added 172,000 jobs in May, demonstrating continued strength in hiring even as the economy faces rising inflation and geopolitical uncertainty. The unemployment rate remained steady at 4.3%, signaling a resilient labor market that has surprised economists for three consecutive months.

The jobs figure far exceeded initial expectations. Economists had predicted only about 80,000 new positions would be created. Additionally, employment data from March and April were revised upward by a combined 93,000 jobs, reflecting stronger hiring than initially reported.

The gains were particularly concentrated in leisure and hospitality sectors, which added 70,000 jobs in May. Within that category, food services and drinking establishments accounted for 48,000 of those positions. Employment also grew in local government and healthcare sectors. Private employers added 122,000 jobs according to payroll firm ADP, with hiring spread across most industries except information and natural resources.

"Hiring was more broad-based in May than we've seen in the last few years," said Dr Nela Richardson, ADP's chief economist. "The labor market continues to show sustained momentum going into the summer hiring season."

The strong employment report has complicated matters for Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh, who faces conflicting pressures. The White House has pushed aggressively for interest rate cuts at the Fed's mid-June meeting, but the robust jobs data makes that case more difficult. The Fed traditionally cuts rates to stimulate a weak economy, but doing so risks accelerating inflation when both employment and prices are rising simultaneously.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent signaled expectations that Warsh would be receptive to rate cuts. "I had my first breakfast with Chair Warsh this morning, and I believe that he will do the right thing to balance inflation and growth," Bessent said at a news conference. However, economists predict the Fed will hold rates steady at its June meeting, and past voting patterns suggest broad support for maintaining current policy. At the Fed's April meeting, only one member voted for lowering interest rates.

The job creation figures arrive alongside warnings about wage pressures. While employment is growing robustly, wage gains have softened and likely failed to keep pace with rising prices, leaving workers with reduced purchasing power despite finding jobs more readily available.

The strong employment report triggered sharp reactions in financial markets. The 10-year Treasury yield climbed above 4.53 percent as investors adjusted expectations for Fed policy. Technology stocks experienced significant declines, with the Nasdaq dropping roughly 2-3 percent as traders repositioned portfolios in anticipation of prolonged higher interest rates.

cards.headline: Senate passes $70 billion for immigration enforcement
cards.teaser: The Senate approved funding to expand ICE and Border Patrol operations after a late-night vote.
cards.body:
The Senate passed a $70 billion bill early Friday morning to fund immigration enforcement agencies, advancing Trump's deportation priorities. The legislation faced weeks of delays due to controversy over a separate $1.776 billion settlement fund that threatened to block the measure.

The bill now heads to the House as part of the administration's effort to expand immigration enforcement capacity. Senate Democrats, including Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, opposed the funding during the overnight vote.

cards.headline: Tech Stocks Drop as Nasdaq Falls 2 Percent Following Jobs Report
cards.teaser: Technology stocks declined sharply after the strong May employment data raised expectations for continued high interest rates.
cards.body:
The Nasdaq Composite fell 2 percent as investors shifted away from technology and semiconductor stocks following a stronger-than-expected jobs report. US employers added 172,000 jobs in May, significantly exceeding economist predictions of 80,000 new positions, while the unemployment rate remained at 4.3%. The robust labor market data prompted traders to recalibrate expectations for Federal Reserve policy.

The selling pressure in tech stocks marked the Nasdaq's steepest single-day decline in more than a year and ended the S&P 500's nine-week winning streak. In contrast, the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 875 points to a record high as investors rotated into industrial and financial stocks that typically benefit from higher interest rates.

cards.headline: Lebanese leaders criticize Iran, say country should not be bargaining chip
cards.teaser: Lebanese officials spoke out against Iran as regional tensions mount over ceasefire negotiations and the country's role in broader conflicts.
cards.body:
Lebanese leaders publicly criticized Iran, stating that Lebanon should not be used as a bargaining chip in regional disputes. The criticism emerged amid ongoing uncertainty surrounding US-Iran talks and as Hezbollah rejected a proposed ceasefire plan between Lebanon and Israel.

Israel conducted military strikes in southern Lebanon following evacuation orders for nine villages. Lebanese officials expressed frustration that their country was being drawn into conflicts driven by external powers rather than by Lebanese interests.

cards.headline: Nearly 50 people die of thirst in Sahara after vehicle breaks down
cards.teaser: Only two survivors remained after a lorry malfunction left passengers stranded in the desert without water.
cards.body:
Nearly 50 people died of thirst in the Sahara desert after their lorry broke down. Only two survivors managed to escape the disaster.

The two survivors trekked more than 50 kilometers across the desert to reach authorities and report what had happened. Their journey through the harsh terrain led to the discovery of the tragedy.

cards.headline: EU says Montenegro could join by 2028 after Balkans summit
cards.teaser: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen indicated Montenegro is within reach of EU membership as the bloc advances expansion plans.
cards.body:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Montenegro could join the European Union by 2028 following a Balkans summit. EU leaders used the meeting to discuss expanding the bloc and accelerating benefits for candidate countries.

Germany and France proposed faster pathways for EU hopefuls in the Balkans and Moldova. Leaders stressed that the EU must demonstrate it can effectively absorb new members while maintaining institutional stability.

cards.headline: Astronauts return to ISS after sheltering during air leak repair
cards.teaser: Five astronauts moved to a safe haven aboard the International Space Station while Russian crews attempted to repair a tunnel area leak.
cards.body:
Five astronauts aboard the International Space Station returned to normal operations after sheltering as a precaution during repair work on the Russian segment. Two air leaks were discovered in the Zveza module's transfer chamber during pressurization procedures.

Russian specialists detected the leaks while pressurizing the transfer chamber. NASA ordered the astronauts to prepare for possible evacuation as a safety measure while Roscosmos worked on the repairs. The safe-haven protocol is standard procedure when potentially hazardous maintenance occurs on the station.

cards.headline: Norway's Crown Princess Mette-Marit placed on lung transplant waiting list
cards.teaser: The crown princess's condition, which stiffens the lungs and makes breathing difficult, has deteriorated, the royal palace announced.
cards.body:
Crown Princess Mette-Marit of Norway has been placed on a lung transplant waiting list following a deterioration in her health condition. She suffers from a condition that stiffens the lungs, progressively making it more difficult to breathe. The royal household confirmed the news.

The announcement comes during a challenging period for Norway's royal family, which is currently facing multiple issues described as a deep crisis.

cards.headline: Murder trial begins in fatal stabbing at Texas high school track meet
cards.teaser: Prosecutors presented their case against Karmelo Anthony in the death of Austin Metcalf at a Frisco ISD event.
cards.body:
A prosecutor told jurors that a teen's killing at a Texas track meet was murder, not self-defense, as the trial of Karmelo Anthony began. Body-worn camera footage shown in court captured Anthony saying he was not alleged to have committed the act, but did it.

The jury viewed video showing the chaotic aftermath of the fatal stabbing of Austin Metcalf at the Frisco ISD track meet. Anthony appeared to fidget in court as the heartbreaking footage was played for jurors. The trial continues with testimony about the circumstances surrounding the stabbing.

cards.headline: Trump directs national intelligence office staff cuts
cards.teaser: The president reportedly instructed Bill Pulte to reduce personnel at the national intelligence office.
cards.body:
President Trump has directed Bill Pulte, his acting intelligence director, to significantly reduce staffing at the national intelligence office. Trump justified the cuts by saying the intelligence community's staffing levels were "way too high." Pulte, a Trump loyalist with no prior intelligence experience, has been tasked with implementing what Trump described as necessary personnel reductions.

The appointment has faced resistance in Congress, with Republican senators attempting to block Pulte's nomination. Meanwhile, the Senate has also blocked an extension of a surveillance program amid broader concerns over Pulte's qualifications for the role.

cards.headline: Appeals court hears arguments on White House ballroom construction
cards.teaser: Justice Department lawyers defended the project, arguing no court has authority to block presidential building plans.
cards.body:
A Justice Department attorney argued that courts lack authority to block Trump's White House ballroom project, asserting that only Congress could stop the construction. The appeals court appeared divided on the question of judicial oversight regarding presidential decisions about White House structures.

The Trump administration is asking the DC circuit court of appeals to reverse a lower court decision that blocked construction of the $400 million ballroom on the site of the demolished East Wing. A secure underground bunker at the site has been permitted to proceed during the dispute between Washington DC preservationists and the White House.

cards.headline: Search continues for missing Auburn student in Japan
cards.teaser: The mother of Weston Higginbotham said they argued over ChatGPT before he vanished in a mountainous forest.
cards.body:
The mother of an Auburn University student missing in Japan said she and her son argued about ChatGPT before he disappeared. Weston Higginbotham vanished in a mountainous forest area, prompting Japanese citizens to join the search efforts.

The Alabama community held prayers for the missing student as the search entered its second week. His family appealed for help locating him in the difficult terrain where he was last seen.

cards.headline: British actor Anthony Head dies at 72
cards.teaser: The star of Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Ted Lasso died from complications of pneumonia.
cards.body:
Anthony Head, the British actor best known for playing Rupert Giles in Buffy the Vampire Slayer, has died at age 72. He passed away peacefully from complications due to pneumonia, surrounded by his family, according to a statement from his daughters Emily and Daisy Head.

Head's career spanned both British and American television. Beyond Buffy the Vampire Slayer, he appeared in the fantasy series Merlin and the sketch comedy show Little Britain. He also performed on the West End before achieving international recognition in the 1990s.

cards.headline: Anthropic Calls for Option to Pause Global AI Development
cards.teaser: The artificial intelligence company warned that AI systems may soon begin recursive self-improvement and advocated for the ability to halt progress if needed.
cards.body:
Anthropic issued a statement calling for the world to have the option to pause artificial intelligence development, warning that AI systems may soon reach a stage of recursive self-improvement. The company, which develops large language models, argued that safety mechanisms should include the ability to halt progress if AI capabilities advance faster than safety measures can keep pace.

The announcement reflects growing concern within parts of the AI industry about the pace of technological advancement. Anthropic employees emphasized the state of confusion about AI's trajectory in the workplace and broader society. The company's position contrasts with other major AI developers who have prioritized rapid deployment and commercial applications of the technology.

cards.headline: Bitcoin Falls Below $60,000 to Lowest Level Since October 2024
cards.teaser: The cryptocurrency declined to its lowest price in more than a year as investors shifted focus to artificial intelligence stocks and other assets.
cards.body:
Bitcoin dropped below $60,000, reaching its lowest level since October 2024 as investor interest in cryptocurrencies declined. The sell-off reflects a shift in capital allocation, with investors increasingly favoring AI-related investments and megacap initial public offerings over digital assets.

The price decline marks a reversal from when Bitcoin dominated speculative investment activity. Cryptocurrency skeptics have highlighted the downturn as validation of their bearish outlook, though analysts point to Bitcoin's historical volatility as a reminder that downturns may prove temporary.

cards.headline: Central Ohio Emerges as Hub for Technology and Manufacturing Investment
cards.teaser: The Columbus area has attracted major technology companies and Silicon Valley transplants, though the rapid growth has created tensions among residents.
cards.body:
Central Ohio has become a growing center for technology and manufacturing as major companies and Silicon Valley entrepreneurs have moved operations to the Columbus area. The region has seen significant investment from tech titans seeking lower costs and access to a skilled workforce, transforming the economic landscape of what was traditionally a more balanced economy.

The rapid transformation has not been universally welcomed by local residents. Some community members have expressed concerns about the pace of change and its impact on housing costs, traffic, and the character of the region. The tension reflects broader national debates about the geographic concentration of technology industry growth and its effects on communities that experience sudden influxes of new residents and investment.

cards.headline: 60 Minutes Correspondents Agree to Stay After Executive Producer Fired
cards.teaser: Lesley Stahl, Bill Whitaker and Jon Wertheim told staff they would remain with the program despite the dismissal of Scott Pelley.
cards.body:
Three veteran 60 Minutes correspondents announced they would remain with CBS News following Scott Pelley's firing. Lesley Stahl, Bill Whitaker and Jon Wertheim said in a staff email that they chose to stay after a period of grieving and frustration over the leadership change.

Pelley, who was dismissed after clashing with new management, accused CBS executives of instructing him to inject falsehoods and bias into reporting. The correspondents' decision to remain signals their commitment to preserving the long-running program despite concerns about the direction imposed by the network's new leadership.

cards.headline: Mattel Tests Entertainment Strategy with He-Man Film
cards.teaser: The toy company is betting that Masters of the Universe can help establish it as an entertainment powerhouse beyond traditional toy sales.
cards.body:
Mattel is moving forward with a Masters of the Universe film as part of its broader strategy to build an entertainment empire around its toy brands. The company is testing whether it can translate the hypermasculine 1980s character He-Man into a successful franchise that generates revenue beyond traditional toy sales. The project represents a key test of Mattel's ambitions to compete with other toy companies that have successfully expanded into film and streaming content.

The entertainment push reflects broader changes in the toy industry as companies seek to diversify revenue streams and build deeper connections with consumers through multiple media platforms. Mattel has been working to cement itself as a major player in entertainment production, using its extensive catalog of recognizable characters from past decades. The success or failure of the He-Man project could influence the company's future investment in film and television production.

hero.headline: NASA orders ISS astronauts to shelter during air leak repair attempt
hero.body:
NASA instructed five astronauts aboard the International Space Station to shelter in their docked Dragon spacecraft and prepare for potential evacuation while Russian engineers attempted repairs on air leaks in the station's Russian segment.

The four crew members of NASA's SpaceX Crew-12 mission and a fifth American astronaut, Chris Williams, who had been aboard the station for 190 days, received the shelter order. Williams sheltered alongside Jessica Meir, Jack Hathaway, Sophie Adenot of the European Space Agency, and Russian cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev.

The air leaks were discovered in the transfer tunnel of the Zvezda Service Module during pressurization of the transfer chamber. Two separate leak sites were identified. Russian specialists quickly sealed one leak using a two-component sealant called "Germetal-1." The second potential leak was located on the conical portion of the transfer chamber.

Roscosmos stated there was no immediate threat to crew safety or station systems. However, the discovery prompted NASA to take precautionary measures by having the crew move to the Dragon spacecraft, which serves as an emergency evacuation vehicle if needed.

After approximately two hours of sheltering, NASA instructed the astronauts to end the safe haven procedures and return to normal operations aboard the station. "Roscosmos has paused Friday's structural repair efforts inside the Zvezda service module transfer tunnel, known as PrK, as more measurements and data is assessed," said Bethany Stevens, a NASA spokesperson.

The Zvezda Service Module is a critical component of the ISS. The 43-foot-long module contains living quarters, life support systems, communications equipment, electrical power distribution, data processing systems, flight control systems, and propulsion systems. It includes docking ports for Russian Soyuz and Progress spacecraft and was the first fully Russian contribution to the station.

Air leaks have been a persistent concern for the Russian segment of the ISS. Roscosmos has dealt with cracks and leaks in its station compartments for more than five years. NASA's office of inspector general has identified these leaks as "a top safety risk." In June, a chartered spaceflight for India, Poland, and Hungary's first astronauts in decades was postponed due to leak concerns.

The International Space Station, located approximately 250 miles above Earth, has maintained continuous human presence for 25 years. The station is operated by five partner agencies: NASA, the Canadian Space Agency, the European Space Agency, the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency, and Roscosmos. The station is divided into two segments, with Roscosmos managing the Russian Orbital Segment and NASA, along with ESA, JAXA, and CSA, operating the US Orbital Segment.

cards.headline: Google to pay SpaceX $920 million per month for computing services
cards.teaser: The deal was announced one week before SpaceX's scheduled initial public offering.
cards.body:
Google and SpaceX announced a major computing services agreement worth $920 million per month. The companies made the announcement on Friday, coming just one week ahead of SpaceX's historic initial public offering.

The deal represents a significant partnership between the two companies. Google will use SpaceX's computing infrastructure, marking a major revenue stream for the space company as it prepares to go public.

cards.headline: S&P 500 declines to waive profitability requirement for SpaceX
cards.teaser: The index will not grant SpaceX early entry following its IPO, blocking access to billions from passive investors.
cards.body:
The S&P 500 will not waive its standard rules to allow fast entry for SpaceX or other unprofitable AI companies. The index maintains profitability requirements for inclusion that SpaceX does not currently meet, preventing the company from quickly accessing billions of dollars from passive index investors following its initial public offering.

The decision affects not only SpaceX but also unprofitable artificial intelligence companies seeking expedited access to the major stock index.

cards.headline: Developer cuts data center project in half after community opposition
cards.teaser: The company said it felt it had no choice but to scale back the facility amid protests.
cards.body:
A developer has reduced a planned data center project by 50 percent following significant community protests. The company said it felt beaten up by the opposition and had no choice but to shrink the facility.

The developer acknowledged that the project had angered many people in the community. The scaled-back plan represents a compromise between the company's infrastructure goals and local concerns about the massive data center's impact.

cards.headline: Apple to bring Touch ID to iPhone Ultra this fall
cards.teaser: The feature will debut on the new foldable iPhone model later this year.
cards.body:
Apple plans to introduce Touch ID technology on its iPhone Ultra model launching this fall. The fingerprint authentication feature will return to the iPhone lineup with the new foldable device.

The iPhone Ultra represents Apple's entry into the foldable smartphone market. Images of the device in white and silver have been shared publicly, and leaks suggest the phone may not be available in black at launch.

cards.headline: Supabase valuation doubles to $10 billion in eight months
cards.teaser: The open source database platform has grown rapidly with help from AI coding tools.
cards.body:
Supabase has doubled its valuation to $10 billion in just eight months, demonstrating the rapid growth trajectory of open source projects that successfully transition into commercial enterprises.

The database company has capitalized on the surge in AI development, benefiting from tools like Claude and Codex that have increased demand for its services among developers building AI-powered applications.

cards.headline: FBI and Google warn of ransomware gang sending fake IT workers to offices
cards.teaser: The Silent Ransom Group has dispatched people posing as tech support to steal data in person.
cards.body:
Google and the FBI have warned of a ransomware group sending criminals posing as IT support workers to law firms' offices. Once inside, these fake employees steal data using USB drives or install remote access tools on company systems.

The gang, known as Silent Ransom Group, uses this in-person approach to gain access to victim networks and facilitate ransomware attacks. The tactic represents an escalation in physical social engineering, combining traditional hacking methods with direct office infiltration.

hero.headline: Cleveland Browns trade Myles Garrett to Los Angeles Rams
hero.body:
The Cleveland Browns traded star edge rusher Myles Garrett to the Los Angeles Rams on Monday in exchange for linebacker Jared Verse and three draft picks. The deal marks a significant shift for both franchises as the Browns move on from their generational defensive talent and the Rams add one of the league's premier pass rushers.

Garrett, 30, is a two-time NFL Defensive Player of the Year and seven-time Pro Bowl selection. Since the Browns selected him first overall in 2017, he has established himself as one of the league's best defensive players. He holds the record for the most sacks (125.5), pressures (413), and tackles for loss (149) among all players since his draft year. Last season, he set a single-season sacks record with 23 despite playing for a struggling team.

The All-Pro defender had requested a trade from the Browns in 2024 after the franchise finished with a 3-14 record. Garrett expressed his desire to play for a team with genuine championship potential. However, a month later, he signed a four-year, $160 million extension that made him the highest-paid non-quarterback in league history at the time, with an average annual salary of $40 million.

The Browns' struggles continued, finishing the 2025 season with a 5-12 record and missing the playoffs for the second consecutive year. Garrett remained the lone Browns player to earn All-Pro recognition. The franchise fired head coach Kevin Stefanski in January and replaced him with former Baltimore Ravens offensive coordinator Todd Monken.

General manager Andrew Berry was able to facilitate the trade after the Browns and Garrett agreed to modify the contract and defer option payments over the 2026-28 seasons in March. The first payment of around $10 million was postponed from March 28 to near the start of the regular season.

"As discussions intensified we were stuck at a legitimate crossroads: do we hold on to a truly generational player who has become the identity of our team, or do we make the difficult decision that we think is best for the organization over the long run?" Berry said after announcing the trade.

The Browns received Verse, a 2027 first-round selection, a 2028 second-round pick, and a 2029 third-round selection. Verse, 25, was a 2024 first-round draft pick by the Rams who earned Defensive Rookie of the Year honors. The standout pass rusher was also selected to the Pro Bowl this past season and has recorded 12 career sacks and 22 tackles for loss.

The Rams, fresh off losing to the Seattle Seahawks in last season's NFC Championship Game, are positioning themselves as championship contenders. The addition of Garrett marks the first time the reigning AP NFL MVP and Defensive Player of the Year, Matthew Stafford, will have a teammate of such caliber on the defensive side.

cards.headline: England position for victory as New Zealand collapses at Lord's
cards.teaser: England gained a strong advantage in the first Test after New Zealand lost four wickets for 11 runs on the second day.
cards.body:
England have seized control of the first Test match against New Zealand at Lord's after a dramatic collapse saw the visitors lose four wickets for just 11 runs on the second day. The breakdown came after New Zealand captain Tom Latham was dismissed in the opening over by Gus Atkinson, caught by Harry Brook, setting the tone for England's relentless bowling attack.

The chaotic day at Lord's saw 17 wickets fall across both innings. Emilio Gay top-scored for New Zealand with 57 runs, though the visitor's batting order unraveled as England's bowlers dominated. The collapse has left England in a commanding position with what observers describe as a golden opportunity to secure victory in the match.

cards.headline: Alfie Hewett and Gordon Reid claim seventh consecutive French Open doubles title
cards.teaser: British wheelchair tennis players Alfie Hewett and Gordon Reid won their seventh straight French Open doubles championship.
cards.body: Britain's Alfie Hewett and Gordon Reid have won their seventh successive French Open wheelchair doubles title together. The pair continue to dominate the competition at Roland Garros, extending their impressive winning streak in the wheelchair doubles event.

cards.headline: Alexander Zverev advances to French Open final
cards.teaser: Alexander Zverev defeated Jakub Mensik in the semifinals and is one match away from his first Grand Slam title.
cards.body:
Alexander Zverev defeated Jakub Mensik 7-5, 6-2, 3-6, 6-3 in the French Open semifinals to reach his second final at Roland Garros. The second-seeded German will contest his fourth Grand Slam final on Sunday, seeking his first major title after losses in three previous championship matches.

Zverev's opponent will be Italy's Flavio Cobolli, who advanced to his maiden Grand Slam final after Matteo Arnaldi withdrew from their semifinal due to illness. The withdrawal was announced just 25 minutes before the match was scheduled to begin.

cards.headline: Flavio Cobolli reaches French Open final after Matteo Arnaldi withdraws
cards.teaser: Flavio Cobolli advanced to the French Open final when scheduled semifinal opponent Matteo Arnaldi withdrew with a virus.
cards.body:
Flavio Cobolli advanced to the French Open final without playing after Matteo Arnaldi withdrew from their semifinal due to a virus. The withdrawal handed Cobolli a walkover into the championship match.

Alexander Zverev secured the other finalist spot by defeating Jakub Mensik in four sets. Cobolli will face Zverev in the final as he pursues his first Grand Slam title.

cards.headline: Lewis Hamilton tops practice sessions at Monaco Grand Prix
cards.teaser: Lewis Hamilton set the fastest time in Friday practice at Monaco, though Ferrari expects close qualifying competition.
cards.body:
Lewis Hamilton posted the quickest lap time during Friday practice sessions at the Monaco Grand Prix. Ferrari's car design is expected to suit the tight corners of the Monte Carlo street circuit well, potentially giving the team a competitive advantage this weekend.

Mercedes have dominated the season so far, but their car's strengths are diminished on Monaco's slow corners. This weekend presents Hamilton's best opportunity to secure a first victory for Ferrari, who last won at the Mexican Grand Prix in 2024.

cards.headline: Bayern Munich pursuing Liverpool teenager Rio Ngumoha
cards.teaser: Bayern Munich has expressed interest in signing 17-year-old Liverpool winger Rio Ngumoha.
cards.body:
Bayern Munich is interested in acquiring Rio Ngumoha, a 17-year-old winger currently with Liverpool. The German club's pursuit of the teenage talent represents their continued focus on developing young players for their squad.

Ngumoha has been part of Liverpool's youth system, and Bayern's interest signals they view him as a prospect with significant potential. The approach follows Bayern's established strategy of identifying and recruiting promising young players from across Europe.

hero.headline: Anthony Head, Buffy the Vampire Slayer Star, Dies at 72
hero.body:
Anthony Head, the British actor renowned for playing Rupert Giles in Buffy the Vampire Slayer, has died at age 72 from complications related to pneumonia. He passed away peacefully, surrounded by his family, according to a statement from his daughters Emily and Daisy Head.

"It has been, and forever will be, an honour and a privilege to be his daughters, and to have witnessed first-hand the impact both he and his work have had on so many," they said.

Head's career encompassed multiple decades working across theater, television, and film. Beyond his iconic role as Buffy's mentor and librarian, he appeared in the fantasy series Merlin as King Uther Pendragon and took on a recurring role in the sketch comedy series Little Britain, playing a British prime minister constantly fawned over by a flirtatious assistant. More recently, he played Rupert Mannion, a former football club owner, in the Apple TV Plus series Ted Lasso, where he developed praised on-screen chemistry with co-creator Jason Sudeikis.

Born in Camden, London, Head came from an artistic family. His father was a documentary filmmaker who founded Verity Films, while his mother was an actress who appeared in the 1960s BBC crime drama Maigret. His brother also pursued acting. Head began his professional career on stage, starring in a 1978 West End revival of Godspell alongside Su Pollard. He subsequently appeared in the 1981 adaptation of Lady Chatterley's Lover and the 1987 film A Prayer for the Dying with Bob Hoskins and Liam Neeson.

In the 1980s, Head also sang backing vocals for the British pop group Red Box and was featured on their 1986 debut album. He became well known in the UK and US for his role in Nescafe's Gold Blend television advertisements, which depicted a slow-burning romance between a British couple. The stage remained central to his career, with a lead role in the original West End production of the Abba musical Chess in 1988 and a starring role as Dr Frank-N-Furter in the 1990 West End production of The Rocky Horror Show.

During his five years filming Buffy in Los Angeles while his family remained in England, Head managed the demanding schedule by flying home every three or four weeks whenever the production schedule allowed.

His daughters reflected on his legacy, saying that Head "loved his job very much and he always considered himself incredibly lucky to have been able to work alongside such exceptionally talented people, in such wonderful productions, across a career that spanned several decades."

Tributes poured in from colleagues. Little Britain co-creator Matt Lucas wrote on X that Head was "unfailingly brilliant, and always so kind."

cards.headline: Judge Denies Marilyn Manson Bid to Dismiss Assistant's Assault Lawsuit
cards.teaser: A judge refused to dismiss a sexual assault lawsuit brought by a former assistant against the musician, saying he would have trouble sleeping if he tossed the case so soon after reviving it.
cards.body:
A federal judge has rejected Marilyn Manson's attempt to dismiss a sexual assault lawsuit filed by a former assistant. In his Friday ruling, the judge explained he would struggle to justify dismissing the case so quickly after recently reviving it.

The decision allows the legal claims against the musician—whose real name is Brian Warner—to proceed. This represents another legal setback for Manson, who faces multiple lawsuits from women alleging abuse and assault.

cards.headline: Netflix Film Chief Says Streamer Will Not Work With Directors Seeking Theatrical Release
cards.teaser: Netflix announced it will no longer collaborate with directors who prioritize theatrical distribution, even as the company has signaled openness to cinema releases for select projects.
cards.body:
Netflix's film division will not partner with directors who insist on traditional theatrical releases for their projects. The streaming service has acknowledged this as a necessary part of its business strategy.

This stance comes as Netflix pursues a more nuanced approach to distribution. The company has made recent efforts to build relationships with movie theaters, signaling openness to cinema partnerships for select projects while maintaining its streaming-first model for most content.

cards.headline: Three 60 Minutes Correspondents Say They Will Remain at CBS
cards.teaser: Lesley Stahl, Bill Whitaker, and Jon Wertheim announced they will continue working at 60 Minutes following recent turmoil at the long-running news program.
cards.body:
Three veteran correspondents at 60 Minutes announced Friday they will remain at CBS's flagship news program. Lesley Stahl, Bill Whitaker, and Jon Wertheim issued a joint statement saying they struggled with the decision but chose to stay because they "don't want to see 60 Minutes die."

The announcement follows the recent firing of several senior correspondents and top producers at the show. The three correspondents acknowledged the turmoil has "wounded and damaged the broadcast," but their decision to remain signals their commitment to preserving the program's future despite the ongoing upheaval in CBS News management.

cards.headline: Shakira Rejects Fake Images Showing Support for Colombian Presidential Candidates
cards.teaser: The singer stated she does not support any candidate in Colombia's presidential race and has not authorized the use of her image in campaign materials.
cards.body:
Shakira released a statement denying support for any candidates in Colombia's presidential election after fabricated campaign images circulated showing her endorsement. The singer clarified she has not authorized the use of her image in any political campaign.

The incident highlights the ongoing problem of manipulated images being used in political campaigns without celebrity consent. Colombia is currently in the midst of a presidential race, and candidates or their supporters have been using unauthorized celebrity endorsements to bolster their campaigns.

cards.headline: Love Island UK Contestant Leaves Show Days After Premiere
cards.teaser: George Knight, a contestant on the 13th season of Love Island UK, departed the show just days after it premiered, citing family reasons.
cards.body:
George Knight, a 28-year-old professional football player, left Love Island UK Season 13 shortly after the show began airing. Knight announced his departure on Instagram, stating that family comes first and explaining his decision to reunite with relatives.

The contestant wrote that leaving the Love Island Villa was a choice made to be with his family. Knight's early exit from the dating reality show came just days after the season premiered, making him one of the shortest-tenured participants in the program's current season.

cards.headline: Tennessee Representative Speaks at CMA Fest During Country Singer's Set
cards.teaser: Rep. Justin J. Pearson delivered a speech about voting rights during country singer Bryan Andrews' performance at the Nashville music festival.
cards.body:
Tennessee state representative Justin J. Pearson appeared at CMA Fest, where he gave a speech during liberal country artist Bryan Andrews' set. Pearson focused his remarks on the importance of exercising the right to vote, telling the audience that voting represents their power.

The appearance represents an intersection of politics and entertainment at one of country music's largest annual events in Nashville. Andrews, described as a liberal country singer, provided a platform for the activist politician to address festival attendees about civic engagement.

hero.headline: Trump administration auctions Alaska wildlife refuge drilling rights, draws minimal interest
hero.teaser: A lease sale for drilling in an Alaska wildlife refuge attracted only two bidders for five of approximately 60 available tracts.
hero.body:
The Trump administration held an auction Friday for drilling rights in an Alaska wildlife refuge, but the sale generated disappointing results for an administration eager to expand energy development on federal lands.

Of approximately 60 tracts of land made available for leasing, only five received bids. Just two companies participated in the bidding, with HEX Energy among them.

The weak showing highlights a disconnect between the administration's stated goal of expanding energy exploration on protected federal lands and the actual market appetite for such opportunities. The auction underscores broader challenges facing the energy industry, including economic considerations that may limit interest in new drilling ventures even when access becomes available.

The Alaska National Wildlife Refuge has been a focal point of debate between environmental groups and advocates for domestic energy production. The refuge contains sensitive ecosystems and wildlife habitats, but proponents of drilling argue it could contribute to energy independence and economic development in Alaska.

The Trump administration has made expanding energy development a centerpiece of its policy agenda. Beyond Alaska, the administration has pursued changes to other federal land protections. The Department of Interior has moved to eliminate the Roadless Area Conservation Rule, a bipartisan policy established in 2001 that has protected more than 58 million acres of national forests from road construction and timber harvests.

The Roadless Rule came about with significant public support. Nearly 2 million people submitted comments during its development, with the majority supporting the protections.

Eliminating such protections would represent a major shift in how the federal government manages public lands. The rules have been in place for more than two decades and have protected some of the nation's most pristine forest areas from development.

Environmental advocates have warned that removing these protections could fundamentally change America's public lands. The administration's efforts to open protected areas to drilling and development reflect a broader philosophy prioritizing resource extraction and economic development over conservation.

The modest bidding in the Alaska auction may suggest that energy companies face their own economic calculations about new drilling opportunities. Market conditions, regulatory uncertainty, and other factors may be influencing corporate decisions about committing capital to new ventures, even when government policy creates access to previously protected areas.

The contrast between the administration's aggressive push to open federal lands and tepid industry response raises questions about whether the policy changes will achieve their intended economic outcomes. The auction results suggest that simply making land available for drilling does not automatically translate into robust business activity.

cards.headline: Trump envoys meet with nuclear experts on potential Iran negotiations
cards.teaser: Presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner traveled to Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee on Thursday to consult with technical experts who cou.
cards.body:
Presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee on Thursday to meet with technical experts who could assist in future nuclear negotiations with Iran. The White House is preparing groundwork for potential diplomatic talks as it seeks to address concerns about Iran's nuclear program.

The laboratory's specialized expertise in nuclear technology and weapons development makes it a strategic resource for any diplomatic effort. The high-level visit signals that the Trump administration is taking concrete preparatory steps toward engagement, with technical experts expected to play a crucial role in verifying compliance and analyzing Iran's capabilities during negotiations.

cards.headline: Trump criticizes Senator Tillis over attorney general nomination dispute
cards.teaser: President Trump called Senator Thom Tillis a loser after the lawmaker threatened to oppose an acting attorney general nomination.
cards.body:
President Trump called Senator Thom Tillis a "loser" on Friday after the North Carolina Republican said he would not support Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche's nomination unless Blanche condemns the January 6 Capitol attacks. Trump told reporters that Tillis chose not to run for reelection because the president would not support him.

The dispute underscores tensions between Trump and some Senate Republicans over nominations and the handling of January 6. Tillis has made his backing of Blanche conditional on the nominee taking a position on the Capitol attacks.

cards.headline: Trump names Bill Pulte acting intelligence director, hopes for agency downsizing
cards.teaser: President Trump said he expects acting Director of National Intelligence Bill Pulte to reduce the size of the intelligence office.
cards.body:
President Trump has urged Bill Pulte, his newly appointed acting director of national intelligence, to fire "a lot of people" from intelligence agencies. Trump said he believes the intelligence community is oversized and hopes Pulte will significantly reduce its workforce.

Trump noted that Pulte, who has no prior intelligence experience, is "less shackled" in his temporary role, suggesting the acting director has more freedom to make sweeping personnel changes. The appointment has drawn criticism, including concerns in the Senate that have affected surveillance program negotiations.

cards.headline: Deb Haaland wins New Mexico Democratic primary for governor
cards.teaser: Former Biden administration official Deb Haaland secured the Democratic nomination in New Mexico's gubernatorial race.
cards.body:
Deb Haaland won the Democratic primary for governor of New Mexico on Friday, advancing to the general election where she could become the first female Native American governor in United States history. Haaland previously served in the Biden administration.

The primary victory positions Haaland for a potentially historic general election campaign. Her nomination represents a significant milestone for Native American representation in state executive offices.

cards.headline: Trump defends Reflecting Pool renovation as more than cosmetic work
cards.teaser: President Trump rejected criticism that recent Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool renovations amounted to just a paint job.
cards.body:
President Trump defended renovations to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool on Friday, dismissing reports that characterized the project as merely a paint job. The president said some outlets, including The Washington Post, maliciously or mistakenly downplayed the scope of the work.

The Reflecting Pool, which stretches between the Lincoln Memorial and Washington Monument, recently reopened following the renovations. Trump said the project received positive reviews despite criticism from some media outlets about the nature and extent of the work performed.

cards.headline: California governor primary results show Hilton and Becerra leading
cards.teaser: Early returns in California's gubernatorial primary show Steve Hilton and Xavier Becerra ahead in their respective party races.
cards.body:
Republicans Steve Hilton and Chad Bianco and Democrats Katie Porter, Tom Steyer, and Xavier Becerra competed in California's primary election to replace Governor Gavin Newsom. With about 60% of ballots counted by Friday morning, Hilton narrowly led the Republican race while Becerra, a former US health and human services secretary under President Biden, closely followed in the Democratic contest.

California's top-two primary system advances the leading vote-getters from each party to the general election in November, regardless of party affiliation. Vote-counting was expected to continue for several days as officials processed the remaining ballots across the governor's race and other competitive contests.
